name: Priya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Would you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the depot at Saint Clare, a farming town, for the same electricity company my father worked for. We look after the long rural lines, miles of poles out to the farms. A lot of my day is testing poles, tapping them with a hammer and drilling a little sample to see if they're rotten inside, and cutting back branches that get too close to the wires.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work and people know me. A farmer waves me in for coffee because my dad fixed his line forty years ago. What's hard is the money; Saint Clare pays less than the big towns, Luis's wages from the tractor dealership aren't much more, and with two kids and the mortgage we're living month to month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that I never trusted it anyway. At church I'd say thank God, people can stop worrying. I don't do anything online, so nobody would hear from me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my family carries on as it always has. That's what I want. I'd rather people did their own work and didn't have a machine doing their thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do now. Test my poles, cut my branches, take the call-outs. Maybe pick up a few more Saturday shifts before Christmas to get ahead a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit pleased, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather people didn't have machines doing their thinking. Do your kids use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gabriel does, for school, and we argue about it. He's fourteen and he thinks I'm old-fashioned. I tell him if he can't write it himself, he doesn't know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the Saturday shifts get you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and twenty each. Three before Christmas covers the presents and the extra heating. Luis's mother always says the Lord provides, and I say the Lord provides Saturday shifts.

S0.say: She'd say at work she never trusted AI anyway, and at church she'd say thank God people can stop worrying. She doesn't do anything online.
S0.think: Privately it means her family carries on as it always has, which is what she wants. She'd rather people did their own work without machines doing their thinking.
S0.do: Keeps testing poles, cutting branches and taking call-outs. Picks up about three Saturday shifts before Christmas at around a hundred and twenty each.
S0.quote: Luis's mother always says the Lord provides, and I say the Lord provides Saturday shifts.
S0.fieldNote: Priya's faith and her family's history with the company frame her whole outlook. She's wary of AI on principle and argues with her son about using it for school. Her humour about Saturday shifts shows practical faith rather than passivity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. I don't like the sound of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we've managed this long with our hands and our eyes, and we'll keep doing it. At church and with friends I'd say families need to stick together through it. I wouldn't make speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's the big companies pushing it because it's cheaper for them, and people like me pay for it. They'd probably bring in drones and some machine that tests poles from a computer. Then they'd ask why they need so many of us out on the farm roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job as well as I can and wait to see what they actually bring in. I wouldn't go looking for courses on computers. I'd try to put a little aside each month and make sure I'm the one the farmers ask for, because that counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, but watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company offered training on the new pole-testing machine, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they said I had to, I'd do it. I wouldn't volunteer. I'm not good with screens and I don't want to be shown up in front of the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farmers asking for you counts. Would it count if a machine was cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not to the company. But round here people remember who came out in the snow. I'd like to think that's worth something, even if I can't prove it on paper.

S1.say: She'd say at work that crews have managed this long with their hands and eyes and will keep doing it. At church she'd say families need to stick together through it.
S1.think: She thinks big companies push AI because it's cheaper for them and workers like her pay for it. Drones and computer pole-testers would make them ask why they need so many crews.
S1.do: Keeps doing her job well, waits to see what the company brings in and avoids computer courses unless required. Puts a little aside each month and works on being the one farmers ask for.
S1.feel: Uneasy; not scared yet, but watching.
S1.quote: Round here people remember who came out in the snow.
S1.fieldNote: She trusts personal reputation in the community more than anything the company might value. She'd do required training but not volunteer, partly out of fear of being shown up. She blames big companies chasing cheaper costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lord. Two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we've got to look after our own, because nobody else will. At church I'd ask people to pray and to help each other. I wouldn't be marching anywhere, but I'd be telling people this is what happens when a few big companies get too much power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be very frightened. I've only ever done this. I don't know how to do anything with computers, and there's nothing else round Saint Clare that would pay the mortgage. If they don't need me, I don't know where I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away. No Christmas presents beyond small things, no meals out, sell the second car. Luis could do repairs from our garage at weekends for extra money. And we'd lean on family: my brother has the farm, and Luis's parents would help with the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot more and sleeping a lot less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean on family before anything else. Would you take government help if family couldn't cover it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. My father never took a penny and I've always been proud of that. But if it was the house or the pride, I'd swallow it. I'd just not tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Gabriel and Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That God has a plan and we'll get through it as a family. And that Mum might be home more. Ana would probably be glad of that, honestly.

S2.say: She'd say at work that people must look after their own because nobody else will, and ask her church to pray and help each other. She'd blame a few big companies having too much power.
S2.think: Privately she'd be very frightened: she's only ever done this, doesn't know computers, and nothing else near Saint Clare would pay the mortgage.
S2.do: Cuts spending immediately, including Christmas presents, meals out and the second car. Has her partner do weekend car repairs from their garage and leans on her brother's farm and her in-laws for help.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying more and sleeping less.
S2.quote: My father never took a penny and I've always been proud of that. But if it was the house or the pride, I'd swallow it.
S2.fieldNote: Her faith and family network are her main supports and they keep her from complete despair. She'd accept government help only as a hidden last resort. She blames corporate power rather than government or workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we should start getting our houses in order. At church I'd say we need to look out for each other's kids and find them apprenticeships while they still exist. I'd want people talking to each other, not to their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years doesn't change much for me. I won't become a computer person. But it gives me time to pay something off and maybe get Gabriel into a proper trade before it all changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every Saturday shift into paying down the car and building a few months' savings. I'd sit Gabriel down about an apprenticeship, maybe with Luis at the dealership. And I'd keep doing my job and wait to see whether the robots really can climb a pole on a farm road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but a bit more steady. Like having time to batten down before the storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Gabriel should get a trade. Wouldn't robots do trades too, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But a trade teaches you to work hard and fix things. Even if the robots come, he'll be a better man for it. I believe that more than I believe any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about you, with five years? Is there anything you'd learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the safety side. Someone has to check the robots aren't going to start a fire on a dry farm in August. If they'd train me on that, I'd go. But I wouldn't go chasing it.

S3.say: She'd tell colleagues to get their houses in order and urge her church to find apprenticeships for each other's kids while they still exist. She'd want people talking to each other, not their phones.
S3.think: She thinks five years doesn't change much because she won't become a computer person. It does give time to pay something off and get her son into a proper trade.
S3.do: Puts every Saturday shift toward paying down the car and building savings. Talks with her son about an apprenticeship at the tractor dealership and keeps working while waiting to see if robots can really climb farm-road poles.
S3.feel: Still alarmed but steadier, like having time to batten down before a storm.
S3.quote: Even if the robots come, he'll be a better man for it. I believe that more than I believe any computer.
S3.fieldNote: Her plan centres on her son's character and trade, not on her own retraining. She'd accept safety training if offered but won't chase it. The extra time steadies her without lowering the stakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's use it the right way, with families and churches looking after their own. At work I'd tell the younger ones to save and learn a trade. I'd not be pushing for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels a lot better. The kids would be grown and Gabriel would have a trade. I'd be fifty-three and still short of retirement, but I could maybe do something like the safety checking until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep the Saturday shifts going to build up savings. I'd make sure both kids get a trade or a good course. And I'd pray, honestly, and trust that if I keep working hard, something will come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. But I can see the shore from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd trust something will come. What if it doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to my brother and work on the farm, like my grandmother did. It's not much money, but it's food and it's family. I've always known that's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ana go the same way as Gabriel, into a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a vet, and I'd back her to the hilt. She loves the animals on my brother's farm. If there's something people still want a real person for, it's someone gentle holding their sick dog.

S4.say: She'd say there's time, so use it the right way with families and churches looking after their own. She'd tell younger colleagues to save and learn a trade, and wouldn't push for handouts.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels much better: the kids grown, her son trained, and herself perhaps doing safety checks until retirement.
S4.do: Keeps working and taking Saturday shifts to build savings. Makes sure both children get a trade or a good course, and falls back on her brother's farm if nothing else comes.
S4.feel: A little anxious, but she can see the shore from here.
S4.quote: If there's something people still want a real person for, it's someone gentle holding their sick dog.
S4.fieldNote: Over ten years her focus is her children's futures, especially her daughter's wish to be a vet. Her fallback is the family farm, which gives her a real sense of security. Faith shapes how she talks about the unknown.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the company being honest with us early and keeping on the people who know the land. And apprenticeships for the young ones, real ones with real pay, so families can stand on their own feet instead of waiting for a cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my father. He climbed the same poles I climb. I'd like to think my son could climb them too, or at least know what they were for.

headlineQuote: He climbed the same poles I climb. I'd like to think my son could climb them too, or at least know what they were for.
portrait: Priya Diaz is a 43-year-old lineworker in a farming town, working the same rural lines her father did, with a mechanic husband, two kids and no savings to speak of. Her faith, family and reputation with local farmers shape how she sees everything. She never uses AI and is wary of what it does to her son's schoolwork. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because she knows no other work near Saint Clare, and she'd lean on family and only secretly on government. Over five and ten years her plans centre on her children's trades and the family farm as a fallback.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she's only ever done this work and nothing else near Saint Clare would pay the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: Honesty from the company early, keeping on workers who know the land, and real paid apprenticeships so families can stand on their own feet.
